# ARC Grid Stream Solving

For isolated ARC-style instances with a test grid, optional demonstrations, and an exact one-action response contract.

## Workflow
1. Parse dimensions, legal values, demo/attempt budgets, and exact action JSON. If one action is required, make the final line valid JSON without extra text.
2. Compare demonstrations cell-by-cell. Distinguish invariant and changed cells, background, retained markers, and introduced colors. Consider local, object/region, directional, count-based, and global rules.
3. Form a rule predicting every changed and unchanged cell in every example, including boundaries. Do not extrapolate from one salient fragment.
4. Treat each demo request as costly information. Request another only if viable hypotheses disagree and a new example could resolve ambiguity.
5. Apply the best-supported rule mechanically to the test. Preserve unaffected cells. Validate row/column counts and legal values before submitting.
6. Choose exactly one legal action: request a demo, submit a grid, or finish only after the instance is over. Never submit a placeholder or uncomputed grid.

## Pitfalls
- A demo consumes budget; it is not a free clarification.
- Sparse patterns can encode different rules; verify against all cells and examples.
- Special markers may persist while a new color extends around/from them; distinguish preservation from recoloring.
- Keep row/column indexing consistent when transcribing larger grids.
- Avoid irrelevant tool calls; use tools only when they concretely help analyze or validate the puzzle.

Use this when demos vary in dimensions, palette, or transformation behavior.

Use this note when full-width colored rows or sparse line marks suggest a tiled/periodic output.

- Treat the seed sequence and its phase as separate unknowns. A sequence containing the right colors can still be wrong if row/column alignment is guessed.
- Read every demo's complete input and output. Record all nonzero line coordinates/colors and map their output coordinates; test whether the output repeats a sequence, whether repeated input colors are significant, and how the phase is anchored.
- Distinguish row-wise periodic filling from diagonal 2D tiling. Inspect neighboring output rows and columns: constant rows support a row-only rule; shifted rows may imply a diagonal/toroidal pattern. Do not transfer the orientation from a different demo without checking the present input geometry.
- For a proposed period p, verify compatibility of every observed marker at its coordinate (including repeated colors and gaps). Enumerate candidate periods and phases when useful; do not select the smallest plausible period unless examples establish that convention.
- A wrong submission falsifies the full rule, including its orientation, period, and phase. Reassess the complete demo set before using another attempt. Avoid serially submitting alternate phases of the same unverified idea.
- Before requesting a demo, articulate what competing hypotheses it will distinguish and how their predicted test outputs differ. Spend the finite budget only for actionable information.
- Mechanically generate the final grid and assert dimensions, widths, and marker compatibility before submitting.

This session demonstrated the risk: several plausible cycles were submitted without being replayed against all demos; later examples showed both constant-row and shifted diagonal tilings, so the test's horizontal-stripe geometry needed explicit validation rather than a guessed phase.", "file_type": ".md", "_source_path": "/home/ubuntu/continual-arc-baselines/.workbench/runs/adhoc-hermesagentlearner-1790545217/attempts/771c27e3136742b79bef1ff131c04e1e/system/state/hermes/skills/reasoning/arc-grid-solving/references/periodic-rule-validation-lessons.md"}
